title: Given a string, find the minimum number of cuts needed so that every resulting piece is a palindrome. Explain how the Palindromic Subsequence pattern combines with a cut dynamic program, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Palindromic Partitioning (Minimum Cuts to Split a String into Palindromes)
keyPoints: Two-layer problem: first build a boolean palindrome table, then run a prefix cut DP on top of it.
The palindrome table uses the same recurrence as the longest palindromic substring: ends match and inner range is a palindrome.
The cut DP defines cuts[i] as the minimum cuts for the prefix ending at index i so every piece is a palindrome.
If the entire prefix [0..i] is a palindrome, cuts[i] is 0; otherwise try every palindromic suffix [j..i] and take 1 + cuts[j-1].
Time and space complexity are both O(n squared).
A string that is already a palindrome needs 0 cuts; a string of all distinct characters needs n-1 cuts.

s1_definition.oneliner: Fewest cuts up to position i is the best over every palindromic piece ending at i of one plus the cuts before that piece.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Palindrome table** precomputed with the boolean DP for O(1) palindrome queries on any range.
- **Cut DP** defines `cuts[i]` as the minimum cuts so the prefix `s[0..i]` splits entirely into palindromes.
- **Recurrence** is: if `pal[0][i]` is true, `cuts[i] = 0`; else `cuts[i] = min over all j where pal[j][i] is true of (1 + cuts[j-1])`.
- **Two-layer structure** means the palindrome table is the reusable building block and the cut array is a classic prefix DP.
- **O(n squared) time and space** for both layers combined.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India breaks long routing strings into the fewest symmetric chunks for a compact storage format. Each chunk must read the same both ways because symmetric chunks compress well. The question is the minimum number of breaks so every chunk is a palindrome.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  String: "AAB" (n=3)

  Layer 1: Palindrome Table
  pal[0][0]=T (A)   pal[1][1]=T (A)   pal[2][2]=T (B)
  pal[0][1]=T (AA)  pal[1][2]=F (AB)
  pal[0][2]=F (AAB)

  Layer 2: Cut DP
  cuts[0]: pal[0][0]=T ── cuts[0]=0
  cuts[1]: pal[0][1]=T ── cuts[1]=0  ("AA" is palindrome, 0 cuts)
  cuts[2]: pal[0][2]=F ── try j:
           j=1: pal[1][2]=F ── skip
           j=2: pal[2][2]=T ── cuts[2] = cuts[1]+1 = 1
           cuts[2]=1

  Answer: cuts[2] = 1  (partition: "AA" | "B")
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Palindromic Partitioning is a two-layer problem that combines the palindrome table from the Palindromic Subsequence pattern with a prefix cut DP. At the National Bank of India, Rajesh uses it to split long routing strings into the fewest symmetric chunks for compact storage. The first layer builds a boolean table that answers whether any range is a palindrome in O(1). The second layer computes the minimum cuts for each prefix.

The cut recurrence is straightforward: if the entire prefix is already a palindrome, zero cuts are needed. Otherwise, for each position, try every palindromic suffix ending there and take one cut plus the minimum cuts for the prefix before that suffix. The answer is in the last position of the cuts array.

The palindrome table is the reusable building block that appears in multiple problems: longest palindromic substring, count of palindromic substrings, and now palindromic partitioning. The cut DP is a classic prefix dynamic program layered on top. Understanding that the two layers are independent and composable is what shows an interviewer you understand the pattern family.

The time and space complexity are both O(n squared). A string already a palindrome needs 0 cuts. A string of all distinct characters needs n-1 cuts. The most common bug is forgetting to check whether the full prefix is a palindrome before trying suffix cuts.

Remember one sentence: build the palindrome table first, then compute minimum cuts for each prefix by trying every palindromic suffix ending there.
